reasons: Clear pass and fail output with an exit code.
Covers each industry and several country values.

terms.meaning: the text sent to a search engine
a search operator that limits results to one domain
the set of words and websites used for one industry
an old bug coming back after a change
matching a word only when it stands alone

sections.name: File setup, failures
sections.title: Header and counters
sections.what: Describes the bug being guarded and sets up the pass count and the list of failures.
sections.why: Tells a reader why the test exists before any check runs.
sections.watch_out: The header says it exits at the first failing set, but it actually records every failure and reports them at the end.

sections.name: check
sections.title: Pass and fail reporting
sections.what: Records each check as a pass or a failure, and prints the detail for failures.
sections.why: One reporting function keeps all checks consistent.
sections.watch_out: Failures are collected rather than thrown, so a broken run still reaches the end.

sections.name: NUCLEAR_MARKERS
sections.title: Nuclear word and domain list
sections.what: Lists nuclear words in English and other languages, plus nuclear regulator and news domains, used to spot leaked nuclear searches.
sections.why: Likely reason: the old bug used these forms, so every form is listed.
sections.watch_out: Matching is by fragment, so an unrelated word containing one of these fragments can trigger a false alarm.

sections.name: findMarkers
sections.title: Finding nuclear words in queries
sections.what: Looks for any nuclear word inside the queries, ignoring case, and returns the words it finds.
sections.why: A simple search that also works for non-Latin scripts.
sections.watch_out: Fragment matching is looser than whole-word matching, so short fragments can match inside other text.

sections.name: findTermLeaks
sections.title: Finding leaked industry words
sections.what: Checks whether another industry's distinctive words appear as whole words in queries, ignoring website filters.
sections.why: Stated in the code: plain substring matching gave false leaks, such as a domain that contains the word mine.
sections.watch_out: Terms containing a dot are skipped here, so domain leaks are not checked by this function.

sections.name: siteFilterDomains
sections.title: Collecting website filters
sections.what: Lists every website named in a site filter across the queries.
sections.why: Lets the checks compare the websites actually used with the allowed list.
sections.watch_out: Only the first site filter in each query is read.

sections.name: JEDDAH
sections.title: Real-estate test project
sections.what: Defines the Jeddah Central Arena test project in Saudi Arabia, with no technology set.
sections.why: Reproduces the project that exposed the original bug.
sections.watch_out: Changing these values changes what the first group of checks covers.

sections.name: NUCLEAR_PROJECT (part 1)
sections.title: Real-estate and nuclear direction checks
sections.what: Defines a nuclear test project, then checks that the real-estate queries contain no nuclear words or filters. Checks that the nuclear queries do contain nuclear words and an authority site filter. Also starts the check that every site filter belongs to its industry.
sections.why: Tests both directions, so the fix does not remove nuclear searches for nuclear projects.
sections.watch_out: The list of nuclear authority sites is fixed, so a new nuclear source needs the pattern updated.

sections.name: NUCLEAR_PROJECT: for
sections.title: Industry site filter sweep
sections.what: Builds queries for every industry across six country values, including none, and checks each site filter is in that industry's allowed list. Then works out each industry's distinctive words, which are words no other industry uses and that are not generic project terms.
sections.why: Checks country-specific regulators too, since they are a separate source of filters.
sections.watch_out: A word counts as distinctive only if no other profile uses it, so shared wording changes which words get checked.

sections.name: NUCLEAR_PROJECT: for
sections.title: Cross-industry leak check and profile coverage
sections.what: Checks that each industry's distinctive words do not appear in queries for other industries, except within the related mining family. Then checks that all ten industries have their own profile and prints the total.
sections.why: Confirms that one industry's vocabulary cannot contaminate another's searches.
sections.watch_out: The related-family exception is hardcoded, so any new related pair must be added by hand.

summary: A regression test that confirms search queries for each industry use only that industry's words and websites, and that real-estate projects no longer get nuclear searches.
purpose: Prevents the earlier defect from returning, where a real-estate project was searched with nuclear words and nuclear websites.
why: The file header names the defect and says the test guards it.
how: Runs five groups of checks: a real-estate project has no nuclear words or filters; a nuclear project does; a missing industry gets neutral queries; every site filter belongs to its own industry; and each industry's distinctive words do not leak into others. Then checks all ten industries have a profile. Prints each result, a total, and exits with code 1 if anything failed.
inputs: The query builder, the industry profile definitions, and a fixed list of nuclear words and domains.
outputs: Printed PASS and FAIL lines, a total, and an exit code of 1 on any failure.
risks: The industry list and nuclear word list are written by hand, so a new industry needs updates here too. Exceptions for related industries are hardcoded.
debug: Each failure message names the offending words or domains. Look at the matching industry in industrySearchProfiles.
